interest: This telegram provides valuable insight into the Nationalist (Kuomintang) government's controversial postwar retention and utilization of General Yasuji Okamura, the former commander-in-chief of the Japanese China Expeditionary Army. Rather than facing immediate prosecution as a major war criminal, Okamura was retained by Chiang Kai-shek's regime as a chief liaison officer to supervise the surrender and repatriation of over a million Japanese soldiers and civilians—a role that also involved behind-the-scenes military consultation against the Chinese Communists. The document illustrates public and journalistic interest in Okamura's mysterious whereabouts in mid-1947, as well as the official Chinese government stance defending his prolonged retention on purely administrative and logistical grounds.
overview: This file consists of an incoming plain telegram dated June 18, 1947, sent from U.S. Ambassador John Leighton Stuart in Nanking to the Secretary of State in Washington, D.C. The telegram reports on a press conference held by the director of the Chinese Government Information Office regarding the whereabouts and current status of former Japanese General Yasuji Okamura. The Chinese spokesperson reaffirmed an earlier statement from April 30, explaining that General Okamura was serving as the chief liaison officer overseeing the Japanese surrender and the repatriation of Japanese forces from China, a task estimated to require several more months to conclude.

subfiles.summary: Ambassador John Leighton Stuart reports from Nanking on the official response to press inquiries concerning the whereabouts and current status of General Yasuji Okamura. At a weekly press conference on June 18, 1947, the director of the Chinese Government Information Office stated that no new details could be added beyond the April 30 statement confirming Okamura's role as chief liaison officer for the surrender and repatriation of Japanese troops. The Chinese government indicated that completing this repatriation work would require several additional months.
